prompt.context: A non-profit hospital wants help to reduce the $10 million loss that the organization has been experiencing in the last 3 years. If the hospital continues this level of loss for more than 2 years, then the hospital endowment would be completely gone and the hospital would need to close its doors.
prompt.question: It is realized that the hospital's loss was due to a new law which basically fixed hospital prices because of the new DRG (diagnosis related groups) hospital payment system in New York State (i.e. price per unit could not be changed). What profitability improvement levers should the team focus on first if the team wants to quickly reduce the hospital's loss? What would you expect to find?

clarifying_info.a: No. Prices are fixed by the new DRG payment system under New York State law — price per unit cannot be changed.

clarifying_info.q: How long has the hospital been losing money?
clarifying_info.a: The hospital has been experiencing a $10 million annual loss for the last 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: How much runway does the hospital have?
clarifying_info.a: If losses continue at this rate for more than 2 more years, the endowment will be completely depleted and the hospital will need to close.

clarifying_info.q: Is this a for-profit or non-profit hospital?

framework: Since price per unit is fixed by law, revenue can only be increased by growing volume (units of service)
Cost structure: distinguish fixed vs. variable costs and identify reduction opportunities
Capacity utilization: assess whether current capacity is over- or under-utilized relative to demand
Short-term lever: cost reduction and capacity rightsizing are faster to execute than demand-side changes
Longer-term lever: revenue growth through increased patient volume (marketing, physician relationships, service mix)

questions.prompt: What profitability levers are available given that price is fixed?
questions.guidance: Strong answer recognizes the profit equation: Profit = (Price × Volume) − Costs. With price fixed, only two levers remain: increase volume or reduce costs. Candidate should prioritize cost and capacity changes as faster levers, then discuss revenue/volume growth as a secondary longer-term strategy.

questions.prompt: On the cost side, what should the team investigate?
questions.guidance: Break costs into fixed and variable. Fixed costs (facility, equipment, core staff) are harder to cut quickly; variable costs (supplies, per-procedure staffing) can be adjusted faster. Shifting the cost structure from predominantly fixed toward more variable reduces break-even risk. Also examine capacity: if the hospital is running beds/ORs below optimal occupancy, rightsizing (e.g., temporarily closing a wing, reducing staff to match actual demand) can cut fixed costs.

questions.prompt: On the revenue/volume side, what marketing questions should the team explore?
questions.guidance: (1) What draws physicians and patients to this hospital, and where do patients come from? Most patients come from surrounding local communities; focusing on underrepresented local neighborhoods can increase volume. (2) How does the hospital compare to competitors on dimensions important to patients and admitting physicians? The hospital was strong on patient care quality but lacked convenience — a gap to address. (3) What are trends in patient care? Trend toward outpatient services (e.g., cataract surgery shifted from 3-day inpatient stay to same-day outpatient procedure) — the hospital could invest in a convenient outpatient facility to capture this growing segment.

brainstorming.prompt: What revenue and cost levers could the hospital pursue to restore profitability?

categories.name: Cost Reduction — Variable Costs
ideas: Reduce supply and pharmaceutical costs through group purchasing or renegotiated vendor contracts
Optimize staffing levels to match actual patient volume (flex staffing)
Reduce overtime by improving scheduling efficiency

categories.name: Cost Reduction — Fixed Costs
ideas: Consolidate or temporarily close underutilized wards or floors
Outsource non-core services (laundry, food service, housekeeping)
Renegotiate facility leases or maintenance contracts

categories.name: Capacity Optimization
ideas: Right-size bed capacity to actual average daily census
Improve throughput (reduce average length of stay) to serve more patients with same capacity
Shift more procedures to lower-cost outpatient settings

categories.name: Volume / Revenue Growth
ideas: Target underrepresented local neighborhoods with outreach programs
Improve physician relations to increase admissions and referrals
Add or expand high-margin outpatient services (e.g., outpatient surgery center)
Improve convenience (parking, scheduling, wait times) to win patients from competitors
Pursue service lines trending toward outpatient care (e.g., cataract surgery, orthopedic procedures)

recommendation: In the short term, focus on cost reduction and capacity rightsizing — specifically, reducing fixed costs by right-sizing staffing and facilities to match current demand, and shifting more costs from fixed to variable to reduce break-even volume

In the medium term, pursue volume growth by targeting underserved local communities, improving convenience for patients and admitting physicians, and investing in outpatient service capabilities aligned with industry trends
risks: Cutting capacity too aggressively could reduce service quality or the ability to handle volume surges
Revenue growth through marketing and outpatient expansion requires upfront investment and takes time to materialize
Two-year runway is tight — execution speed is critical
next_steps: Conduct a detailed cost breakdown to identify the largest fixed-cost buckets and quick-win reductions
Analyze capacity utilization by unit/service line to identify consolidation opportunities
Commission a patient origin and referral analysis to prioritize volume growth initiatives
Evaluate feasibility and economics of an outpatient facility investment
